claim: Blue/Green Deployments suit major or minor engine version upgrades, operating system updates, schema changes that do not break logical replication, and parameter changes, with short, predictable downtime.
q: When should you use Amazon RDS Blue/Green Deployments?
d: major or minor version database engine upgrades
ev: f

Blue/Green Deployments are ideal for use cases such as major or minor version database engine upgrades, operating system updates, schema changes on green environments that do not break logical replication, like adding a new column at the end of a table, or database parameter setting changes.
f
This allows you to stay current on security patches, improve database performance, and access newer database features with short, predictable downtime.

claim: In Blue/Green Deployments the blue environment is the current production environment and the green environment is the staging environment that becomes production after switchover.
q: What are the blue and green environments in RDS Blue/Green Deployments?
d: blue environment is your current production environment
ev: f

In Amazon RDS Blue/Green Deployments, the blue environment is your current production environment. The green environment is your staging environment that will become your new production environment after switchover.

claim: A Blue/Green switchover blocks writes to both environments until it completes, lets green catch up, redirects traffic to green, and only then enables writes on green, so no data is lost.
q: How does an RDS Blue/Green Deployments switchover work?
ev: f

When Amazon RDS Blue/Green Deployments initiate a switchover, they block writes to both the blue and green environments, until switchover is complete. During switchover, the staging environment, or green environment, catches up with the production system, ensuring data is consistent between the staging and production environment.
f
Blue/Green Deployments are designed to enable writes on the green environment after switchover is complete, ensuring zero data loss during the switchover process.

claim: After switchover, Blue/Green Deployments do not delete the old production environment, and it keeps incurring standard charges until you delete it.
q: What happens to the old production environment after an RDS Blue/Green switchover?
d: do not delete your old production environment
ev: f
Amazon RDS Blue/Green Deployments do not delete your old production environment.
f
Standard billing charges apply on old production instances until you delete them.

claim: During a Blue/Green deployment you pay approximately 2x the cost of running the workload, because green instances cost the same as blue instances.
q: What does an RDS Blue/Green deployment cost while it runs?
ev: f
Effectively, you are paying approximately 2x the cost of running workloads on db.instance for the lifespan of the blue-green-deployment.

scope: per Blue/Green switchover, maximum tolerable downtime setting
claim: You can set the maximum tolerable switchover downtime as low as 30 seconds; a switchover times out if an ongoing transaction exceeds it.
q: How low can you set the maximum tolerable downtime of an RDS Blue/Green switchover?
ev: f
You can specify your maximum tolerable downtime, as low as 30 seconds, and if you have an ongoing transaction that exceeds this your switchover will time out.

claim: The FAQ says Blue/Green Deployments do not support Global Databases, RDS Proxy, cross-Region read replicas or cascaded read replicas.
q: Which topologies does the RDS FAQ say Blue/Green Deployments do not support?
d: do not support Global Databases, Amazon RDS Proxy
ev: f
No, Amazon RDS Blue/Green Deployments do not support Global Databases, Amazon RDS Proxy, cross-Region read replicas, or cascaded read replicas.
note: FAQ versus guide: blue-green-deployments-considerations may now list RDS Proxy (and possibly other topologies) as supported. The decisions+changes lens owns the guide page; record the conflict there and teach the guide.

claim: Blue/Green Deployments cannot be used to roll back changes.
q: Can you roll back with RDS Blue/Green Deployments?
d: you cannot use Amazon RDS Blue/Green Deployments to rollback
ev: f
No, at this time you cannot use Amazon RDS Blue/Green Deployments to rollback changes.

claim: The FAQ lists Blue/Green Deployments for Aurora MySQL, Aurora PostgreSQL, RDS for MySQL, RDS for MariaDB and RDS for PostgreSQL.
q: Which engines support RDS Blue/Green Deployments?
ev: f

Amazon RDS Blue/Green Deployments are available in Amazon Aurora MySQL-Compatible Edition, Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL-Compatible Edition, Amazon RDS for MySQL, Amazon RDS for MariaDB, and Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL.

claim: RDS Optimized Writes gives RDS for MySQL up to 2x improved write transaction throughput, at no additional cost.
q: What does RDS Optimized Writes give RDS for MySQL?
d: up to 2x improved write transaction throughput
ev: f
All Amazon RDS for MySQL users should implement Amazon RDS Optimized Writes for up to 2x improved write transaction throughput.
f
Amazon RDS Optimized Writes are available to RDS for MySQL customers at no additional cost.

claim: RDS Optimized Reads places MySQL and MariaDB temporary objects on NVMe-based instance storage instead of the EBS volume, speeding up complex query processing by up to 2X.
q: How do RDS Optimized Reads speed up queries?
ev: f

Optimized Reads place temporary objects on the database instance's NVMe-based instance storage, instead of the Amazon Elastic Block Store volume. This helps to speed up complex query processing by up to 2X.

claim: The RDS console can set up the network connection between a Lambda function and an RDS or Aurora database, and AWS recommends using RDS Proxy for that connection.
q: How should a Lambda function connect to an RDS database?
d: We recommend that you use RDS Proxy
ev: f
On the RDS console, select an RDS or Aurora database from the database list page, and choose “Set up Lambda connection” from the "Action" menu.
f
We recommend that you use RDS Proxy during this connection set up.

claim: When you choose to connect to an EC2 compute resource while creating a database, RDS automates the networking setup, such as security groups, subnets and ingress and egress rules.
q: How can the RDS console connect a new database to an EC2 instance?
d: Connect to an EC2 compute resource
ev: f

When you select this option, Amazon RDS automates the manual networking set up tasks such as creating a VPC, security groups, subnets, and ingress/egress rules to establish a connection between your application and database.
f
On the “Create database” page, select “Connect to an EC2 compute resource” option in the Connectivity Section.

claim: AWS Config can continuously record configuration changes to RDS DB instances, DB subnet groups, DB snapshots, DB security groups and event subscriptions, and AWS Config rules can check them.
q: How can you monitor configuration changes to Amazon RDS resources?
ev: f

You can use AWS Config to continuously record configuration changes to Amazon RDS DB Instances, DB Subnet Groups, DB Snapshots, DB Security Groups, and Event Subscriptions and receive notification of changes through Amazon Simple Notification Service (SNS).
f
You can also create AWS Config Rules to evaluate whether these Amazon RDS resources have the desired configurations.

claim: IAM policies can reference RDS resources such as DB instances, snapshots, read replicas and parameter groups, and tags can be used in IAM policies to control actions on resources with the same tags.
q: How do you control which actions users can take on specific Amazon RDS resources?
ev: f
You do this by referencing the Amazon RDS resources in the AWS IAM policies that you apply to your users and groups.
f

By using tagging, you can categorize your resources (e.g. "Development" DB instances, "Production" DB instances, and "Test" DB instances), and write AWS IAM policies that list the permissions (i.e. actions) that can be taken on resources with the same tags.
